definition: The central sulcus is a brain region measured in this study as part of the modality-specific “spokes” involved in semantic processing. Its activity was linked especially to identifying manmade objects, consistent with a contribution from motor-related cortex when object knowledge is retrieved.

reasons: The definition adds an unsupported interpretation that central sulcus activity reflects “motor-related cortex when object knowledge is retrieved”; the packet only says motor cortex contributed to identification of tools/manmade objects, not retrieval of object knowledge.
The phrase “brain region” is imprecise for this term in the source, which identifies the central sulcus as a measured site (CS) rather than defining it as a cognitive construct.

The definition claims that central sulcus activity is “consistent with a contribution from motor-related cortex when object knowledge is retrieved,” but the packet only states that motor cortex contributes to identification of tools; it does not directly connect central sulcus activity to motor-related cortex or retrieval of object knowledge in that explicit manner.

While the packet supports that central sulcus was measured as part of modality-specific ‘spokes’ and that CS showed stronger later effects for specific-level identification of manmade objects, the motor-related consistency clause is an extra interpretive linkage not clearly supported in the provided text.
